Evaluation of the Orthopaedic Patient
Undergoing Cancer Therapy

OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess the multiple-hit hypothesis for patients with cancer.
Determine what cancer treatments will increase a patient’s risk for osteopenia and
osteoporosis.
Identify late complications of chemotherapy that may affect patients with a history of cancer.
Introduction
Patients with cancer are surviving longer and developing routine illnesses, such as fractures
and degenerative joint disease.
Treatment may result in long-term adverse effects that affect surgical decision making.

Orthopaedic treatment of patients with cancer/patients who are cancer survivors must involve
consideration of the cancer and treatment adverse effects.
Patients with cancer may have a multitude of risk factors that contribute to overall frailty and
morbidity (multi-hit hypothesis).
The more remote the cancer history, the less likely adverse effects.
Patients with a complex cancer treatment history or multiple medical comorbidities may
benefit from a comprehensive perioperative medical evaluation.
Role of the Orthopaedic Surgeon

Role of the Orthopaedic Surgeon
As cancer therapies continue to evolve, more patients are surviving cancer and living
with stable metastatic disease. These advancements in cancer care pose previously
unseen challenges in medical and surgical care of patients. Because the cancer itself is
stable from an oncologic perspective, routine medical issues, such as fractures, continue
to affect patients. A patient who was cured of cancer many years ago may have several
lingering adverse effects from the cancer or its management. Osteopenia and
osteoporosis from prior therapy are examples. Prior to surgical treatment in patients
with cancer or who have a history or cancer, orthopaedic surgeons must perform a
through perioperative evaluation to adequately understand the perioperative risks.
Although healthcare delivery transforms, fewer surgeons are a hospital’s primary service
attending of record for surgical patients. Increasingly, patients are treated in the hospital
by internal medicine or family medicine trained hospitalists with surgical co-
management models. Although many of the medical issues are being addressed by
other specialties, the orthopaedic surgeon must understand the complex interplay of
multiple medical conditions to provide optimal care for patients. A discussion of the
management of musculoskeletal tumors is beyond the scope of this lesson. For
additional information, please refer to Resource 1.
Multiple-hit Hypothesis for Patients With Cancer or With a History of
Cancer


Multiple-hit Hypothesis for Patients With Cancer or With a History of
Cancer
Dissimilar from a relatively healthy woman with a fall-induced hip fracture necessitating
arthroplasty, her twin with breast cancer who sustains the same fall-induced hip fracture
may have different outcomes because of her treatment history. The twin with cancer is
more likely to be deconditioned and frail from the combined effects of the cancer and
prior treatment. Therefore, the surgeon must be mindful of potential complications. The
multiple-hit hypothesis for cancer deconditioning illustrates the many conditions that
lead to deconditioning in patients with cancer1 (Figure 1). Orthopaedic surgeons must
be aware that these conditions may affect outcomes and may consider delaying elective
procedures to address some of these concerns via medical optimization and pre-
rehabilitation.
Figure 1 Diagram shows the multiple-hit hypothesis for cancer deconditioning.
(Reproduced with permission from Sahai SK, Ismail H: Perioperative implications of
neoadjuvant therapies and optimization strategies for cancer surgery. Curr Anesthesiol
Rep 2015;5[3]:305-317.)

Time Elapsed Since Most Recent Cancer Episode

Time Elapsed Since Most Recent Cancer Episode
In general, the more distant in time the most recent cancer episode, the less likely it will
play a role in medical or surgical decision making. However, some prior treatment
options may increase a patient’s risk for osteopenia and osteoporosis, leading to
fractures requiring surgical management.
Perioperative Consultation with Specialists

Perioperative Consultation with Specialists
As therapies evolve, patients with cancer will continue to have complex treatment
histories that may or may not affect perioperative outcomes. Many institutions have
comprehensive perioperative medicine programs that are staffed by internal medicine–
trained and anesthesiology-trained physicians. Early referral to these programs may aid
in clarifying risks and advantages of elective procedures. For more urgent procedures, a
comprehensive risk assessment with clear perioperative recommendations may be
invaluable for surgical planning and outcomes. If a comprehensive perioperative
evaluation is not available, the surgeon may need to request a formal evaluation from
the patient’s primary care physician. Note that perioperative medical evaluations are not
medical clearances for surgery, and the use of the phrase cleared for surgery with
patients is discouraged because it conveys the belief that nothing will go wrong, even in
high-risk procedures. Optimization is a better term. For patients undergoing active
cancer treatment or within the posttreatment surveillance period, preoperative
consultation with the treating oncologist is highly recommended. In these situations,
orthopaedic surgeons should ask colleagues about medical issues and adverse effects
the cancer history may pose for the planned orthopaedic procedure.

Medical Comorbid Conditions
Perioperative risk calculators can be used to estimate medical risk for a given procedure.
Traditionally, these calculators focus on cardiovascular risk and usually do not account for
cancer history.
Patients with cancer have a risk for deconditioning and frailty.
Older patients should undergo a comprehensive geriatric assessment.
Preoperative functional status predicts postoperative complications.
Patients with cancer have a risk for premature osteopenia and osteoporosis.
Perioperative Risks

Perioperative Risks
Perioperative risk assessment has revolved around the concept of preventing or
minimizing major adverse cardiac complications, specifically perioperative myocardial
infarction. The Revised Cardiac Risk Index and the Gupta Perioperative Risk Assessment
calculators are widely used and consider the following comorbid conditions: high-risk
surgery, history of ischemic heart disease, history of congestive heart failure, history of
cerebrovascular disease, use of insulin for diabetes mellitus, and elevated creatinine
level. These calculators estimate only cardiovascular risk for procedures and do not
estimate the risk for other potential complications, such as pneumonia, wound infection,
venous thrombosis, or delirium.2 Although time-consuming, use of the more
comprehensive American College of Surgery National Surgical Quality Improvement
Program Surgical Risk Calculator in complex situations is warranted as a starting point
for discussions about risk and shared decision making.3
Deconditioning/Frailty

Deconditioning/Frailty
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:06 PM
AAOS | Evaluation of the Orthopaedic Patient Undergoing Cancer Therapy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003008
5/20

Patients with cancer are at risk for physical deconditioning caused by various factors1
(Figure 1). Treatment adverse effects may linger for months and years; therefore,
patients with cancer may be more frail than others in the same age cohort. As patients
age and more elderly patients are being treated via more aggressive treatment options,
the concerns about frailty must be addressed. A frail patient will have a more
complicated perioperative course than his or her counterpart who likely is more active.
The American Society of Clinical Oncology and the International Society of Geriatric
Oncology recommend a comprehensive preoperative geriatric evaluation in at-risk
populations. From an orthopaedic perspective, a frail patient may not be able to perform
rehabilitation postoperatively, delaying placement and return to the desired place of
discharge. A frail patient may need to be placed in a skilled nursing facility rather than be
discharged home. Therefore, post-discharge placement discussions should occur before
surgical scheduling, if possible.
Functional Status Assessment

Functional Status Assessment
Orthopaedic surgeons are acutely aware that presurgical functional status predicts
postoperative functional outcome. An athlete who sustains a femur fracture is more
likely to have a successful functional recovery than a sedentary patient with the same
injury. More recent literature also advances the idea that preoperative functional status
predicts postoperative medical outcomes, such as cardiac events, and that validated
survey instruments such as the Duke Activity Score Index, be used rather than subjective
measures of functional status.4
Osteopenia and Osteoporosis

Osteopenia and Osteoporosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:06 PM
AAOS | Evaluation of the Orthopaedic Patient Undergoing Cancer Therapy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003008
6/20

Patients with cancer are at risk for premature bone loss caused by treatment. In many
patients, bone loss is accelerated and places the patient at risk for fractures after falls.
For example, prior use of aromatase inhibitors—anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane
—inhibits androgen to estrogen conversion and may lead to premature bone density
loss. Androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer also places men at increased risk
for bone density loss and osteoporosis. Chemotherapies such as doxorubicin,
methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, and 5-fluorouracil may lead to premature menopause
and subsequent premature bone loss in premenopausal women. Similarly,
oophorectomy for ovarian cancer in premenopausal women leads to premature
menopause and its resultant adverse effect of osteopenia. Corticosteroids are widely
used in cancer treatment, and prolonged use has been associated with loss of bone
mineral density.
Figure 2 shows the relative amount of bone loss resulting from certain therapies. The
American Society of Clinical Oncology published guidelines on screening and
management of cancer-related bone loss.5

Treatment History: Surgery and Radiation Therapy
Assess for cancer surgery–related long-term complications or adverse effects.
Assess for radiation therapy–related long-term complications or adverse effects.
Functional Disability from Prior Surgery


Functional Disability from Prior Surgery
Patients with a history of cancer surgery should be questioned about any ongoing issues
that may affect recovery. For example, patients with colostomies for colorectal surgery
may be at risk for malnutrition, whereas patients with a history of adrenalectomy may be
at risk for perioperative adrenal insufficiency.
History of Perioperative Complications

History of Perioperative Complications
A thorough history and physical examination should include any history of surgery and
any complications that may have occurred. From an anesthetic perspective, this should
include any airway complications or anesthesia-related concerns. From a medical
perspective, unexpected transfusions, pulmonary and/or cardiac complications, and
prolonged hospital lengths of stay should be considered.
History of Radiation Therapy
Cardiovascular Complications
Orthopaedic surgeons must be aware that radiation therapy may accelerate atherosclerosis
and lead to premature coronary artery or carotid artery disease. In patients in whom radiation
is aimed near the heart, conduction abnormalities also may occur.6
Pulmonary Complications
Orthopaedic surgeons must be mindful that radiation therapy targeted to the lungs may lead
to radiation pneumonitis and eventually pulmonary fibrosis. In otherwise asymptomatic
patients, no workup is necessary.6

Treatment History: Chemotherapy
Overview
Chemotherapy agents may have cardiotoxic adverse effects, including heart failure, ischemia,
and arrythmias.
Chemotherapy agents may have pulmotoxic adverse effects, including fibrosis or pleural
effusions.
Impaired renal function is a common adverse effect of certain cancer treatment regimens.
Patients with cancer have a risk for venous thromboembolism and bone marrow failure.
Immunotherapy-related adverse effects may persist for as many as 2 years after treatment.
Steroids often are used as adjunct therapy in the management of cancer and may lead to bone
loss.

Overview
A complete review of chemotherapy complications and adverse effects that may pose
concerns in the perioperative period is beyond the scope of this lesson. A summary of
potential concerns that should be considered in patients with a history of chemotherapy
is provided. Chemotherapy complications tend to be class specific; therefore, similar side
effects are expected within the same class of drugs.
Cardiovascular Complications

Cardiovascular Complications
In practice, cardiotoxicity from chemotherapy may manifest as multiple etiologies,
including cardiac dysfunction, cardiac ischemia, cardiac arrhythmias, and fibrosis and
pericarditis. The risk of cardiotoxicity is higher in patients with preexisting cardiovascular
risk factors (eg, smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus), female patients, patients
older than 70 years, patients who have undergone multiple chemotherapies, and

patients who have undergone radiation therapy to the mediastinum. Figure 3 illustrates
various cardiotoxic side effects that may affect patients.7
Figure 3 Illustration shows the cardiovascular side effects of chemotherapy and
radiation therapy. HER-2 = human epidermal growth factor receptor 2. (Reproduced with
permission from Lenneman CG, Sawyer DB: Cardio-oncology: An update on
cardiotoxicity of cancer-related treatment. Circ Res 2016;118[6]:1008-1020.)
Pulmonary Complications

Pulmonary Complications
Pulmonary complications from chemotherapy may result from direct cytotoxicity to the
lungs, oxidative damage, or disruption of collagen synthesis. Pulmonary toxicity may
result from bleomycin, cyclophosphamide, nitrosoureas, mitomycin, busulfan, and
methotrexate. Diagnosis of pulmonary toxicity may be difficult because of a large
differential diagnosis of respiratory symptoms. In practice, pulmonary toxicities may
manifest as pneumonitis and fibrosis (monoclonal antibodies, alkylating agents) and
effusions (docetaxel and tyrosine kinase inhibitors). Patients who are visibly short of
breath on presentation with minimal activity should be referred for additional
evaluation. Patients who are asymptomatic and able to exercise at moderate levels of
activity without pulmonary complaints do not require additional evaluation.

Renal Complications

Renal Complications
Nephrotoxic effects of chemotherapy are most likely to occur with the platinum
subgroup of alkylating agents, which includes cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin.
Nephrotoxicity may develop in as many as 30% of patients receiving cisplatin. The
syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion occurs in 1% to 2% of
patients with cancer. Chemotherapeutics such as vincristine, vinblastine, and
cyclophosphamide occasionally may be implicated as a cause of this syndrome.
Hematologic Complications

Hematologic Complications
Chemotherapy is known to cause anemia in patients with cancer via direct bone marrow
suppression. Myelosuppression and pancytopenia usually are reversible after 1 to 6
weeks of stopping therapy, but they may persist longer in some patients. Because of
their hypercoagulable state, patients with cancer have an increased risk for venous
thromboembolism. Patients with multiple myeloma who are being treated with
thalidomide have a higher risk for thrombotic complications; therefore, many are being
treated via preventive anticoagulation during treatment.
Immunotherapy (Early and Late Effects)

Immunotherapy (Early and Late Effects)

The field of immunotherapy and targeted chemotherapy has rapidly evolved in the past
decade. Immune checkpoint inhibitors have made strides in the management of solid
tumors but are associated with considerable adverse effects. Adverse effects in this class
of drugs are known as immune-related adverse effects and may include pruritis,
dermatitis, colitis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, adrenal insufficiency,
pneumonitis, renal failure, myasthenia gravis, uveitis, episcleritis, Guillain-Barré
syndrome, neuropathy, meningitis, encephalitis, transverse myelitis, myocarditis,
pericarditis, arthritis, and myositis8 (Figure 4). Management of these adverse effects
requires special knowledge; therefore, the treating oncologist must be consulted if
adverse effects occur. Immune-related adverse effects may occur as late as 24 months
after treatment. Surgical management of patients being treated via immunotherapy
should be coordinated with the treating oncologist to determine timing and possible
interruption of treatment.
Figure 4 Illustration shows representative immune-related adverse events observed with
immune checkpoint blockers. (Adapted with permission from Ventola CL: Cancer

Adjunct Therapy (Steroids)

Adjunct Therapy (Steroids)
Orthopaedic surgeons are aware of the risk chronic steroid use poses to patients with
regard to bone density. Many patients with cancer receive steroids as adjuncts to
treatment to manage adverse effects or to manage nausea. Osteonecrosis is a well-
known adverse effect in patients who have undergone therapy with high-dose steroids
for lymphoma, testicular cancer, or other tumors. Stress-dose steroids have been widely
prescribed for the perioperative treatment of surgical patients; however, more recently,
this practice has come under scrutiny, and guidelines for the perioperative
administration of steroids have recommended a more proscribed and restrictive
approach.
Active Cancer/Stable Metastatic Cancer
Oncologic Consultation
Patients with active cancer or stable metastatic disease should not undergo elective surgery
until evaluated by their treating oncologist.
Orthopaedic surgeons should be prepared to offer palliative surgical treatment options for
patients with a pathologic fracture.

Oncologic Consultation
In patients with active cancer or stable metastatic cancer who have an unrelated
orthopaedic surgical issue, a multidisciplinary meeting should be held with the treating
oncologist to determine the risks and advantages of surgical treatment. For elective

procedures, delaying surgical treatment to incorporate a pre-rehabilitation program and
medical optimization until after treatment is complete may lead to better outcomes. In
For urgent procedures, risk must be clearly explained to the patient. For example,
patients treated via immunotherapy may have immune-related adverse effects, such as
myocarditis, requiring high-dose suppressive steroid therapy that may affect wound
healing postoperatively. In addition, a severely deconditioned patient with poor
performance status may do well intraoperatively; however, postoperative recovery and
placement may pose a challenge. In these patients, all possible therapeutic options,
including nonsurgical management, should be documented with the associated risks and
advantages.
Palliative Therapy

Palliative Therapy
Orthopaedic surgeons may be called on to perform palliative procedures, such as
surgery to manage an impending pathologic fracture caused by bone metastasis. The
surgical procedure may not prolong a patient’s life but may improve the patient’s quality
of life. Depending on the risks involved, the surgeon may need to alter the approach and
plan for surgery.
Advanced Care Planning

Advanced Care Planning
Orthopaedic surgeons rarely are called into advanced care planning conferences;
however, their insight may prove invaluable to the treating team if metastatic bone
disease is present and pathologic fractures are expected. Orthopaedic surgeons can
explain the expected postoperative recovery course for a given procedure to the patient

and help the team determine if surgical treatment is an option given the patient’s
treatment goals.
Anticipating Postoperative Complications
Overview
Certain chemotherapy agents are associated with poor wound healing and wound dehiscence.
Patients being treated with these agents should discuss the optimal timing of elective
procedures with their treating oncologist.
Patients with cancer/patients who are cancer survivors have a higher risk for postoperative
venous thromboembolism.
Although rare, postoperative delirium may occur in patients with cancer because of chemo-
brain. Research in this area is ongoing.
Because of cancer deconditioning and frailty, discharge planning may be different for patients
with cancer.
Wound Healing

Wound Healing
If a patient has received bevacizumab for the management of cancer, any surgical
procedures should be delayed for approximately 6 to 8 weeks from the last dose to
minimize the risk of wound dehiscence. Similarly, tyrosine kinase inhibitors and mTOR
inhibitors may affect wound healing. Therefore, the timing of surgical treatment,
especially for elective procedures, should be discussed with the treating oncologist.
Radiation therapy poses a unique risk for delayed wound healing in the postoperative
period. For example, 30% of patients who undergo preoperative radiation therapy for
soft-tissue sarcoma of the extremities experience wound complications, such as the
need for secondary surgical procedures, readmission, and prolonged dressing changes.

Surgeons should educate the patient about these possible complications if radiation and
surgical fields overlap.9
Venous Thromboembolism

Venous Thromboembolism
Patients with cancer have a high risk for postoperative deep vein thrombosis. The
American Society of Clinical Oncology recommends extended deep vein thrombosis
prophylaxis in patients at high risk for deep vein thrombosis. Patients undergoing upper
extremity procedures may not require an extended course of treatment if ambulation is
recovered quickly; however, for those undergoing lower extremity procedures in which
ambulation may be restricted, extended deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis with low-
molecular-weight heparin is recommended.
Postoperative Delirium

Postoperative Delirium
Orthopaedic surgeons are familiar with postoperative delirium in elderly patients. This
complication also may occur in the cancer patient population. Currently, data on the
effects of chemo-brain and the incidence of postoperative delirium are limited.
Discharge Planning

Discharge Planning
SEND FEEDBACK

During the initial consultation with the patient, orthopaedic surgeons should discuss the
entire anticipated course of care. Often, patients think they will be discharged home
postoperatively, only to discover that they must be discharged to a skilled nursing
facility.
Summary/Outcomes
Oncologic treatment of cancer patients is rapidly evolving. Orthopaedic surgeons are not
expected to understand all the nuances of treatment and their adverse effects that may affect
the procedure being considered. However, orthopaedic surgeons are expected to understand
when to call for assistance from anesthesia, internal medicine, and oncology colleagues if
concerns arise.
